oneSentence: False or misleading content can spread by mistake or on purpose, and the difference matters because intent changes how we respond.
plainExplanation:
These terms describe information problems, not a single technology. Misinformation is false or misleading content shared without an intent to mislead. Disinformation is false or misleading content created or shared with the aim of misleading people. Both can appear as text, images, audio or video, including content made with generative AI.

What goes in can be a rumour, a copied post, an edited image, a synthetic voice clip, or a video taken out of context. What happens next is that the content is created, altered, reposted or recommended, often moving faster than checking. What comes out is confusion, a false belief, or a damaged reputation, and sometimes real-world harm.

The key difference is intent. If someone forwards the wrong evacuation time because they believed it, that is misinformation. If someone fabricates the time to cause panic, that is disinformation. In practice, intent can be hard to prove, so people sometimes use the broader phrase “misinformation and disinformation” together.

These terms are often confused with deepfakes and hallucinations. A deepfake is one possible form of synthetic media, often audio or video, that may be used for misinformation or disinformation but is not the whole problem. A hallucination is a model output that is false or unsupported; it becomes misinformation only if someone shares it as if it were true, and disinformation only if it is used deliberately to mislead.

everydayAnalogy.title: A confusing message in a group chat
everydayAnalogy.story: In a school trip group chat, Amina writes, “Samir said he cannot come because he is sick.” Several people are unsure whether “he” means Samir or the bus driver mentioned earlier. Luis guesses it means the driver and tells others the trip might be cancelled. Later, one student who wants the trip postponed repeats the same claim even after seeing the teacher’s correction. The same unclear message led first to an honest mistake and then to deliberate spreading of a false claim.

mapping.analogyElement: An ambiguous message with an unclear “he”
mapping.aiElement: A piece of content that is easy to misread or take out of context

mapping.analogyElement: Luis repeating the wrong meaning because he guessed
mapping.aiElement: Misinformation shared without intent to mislead

mapping.analogyElement: The student repeating the false claim after seeing the correction
mapping.aiElement: Disinformation spread with intent to mislead
Fact-checking often moves more slowly than sharing

everydayAnalogy.limitation: This analogy uses ambiguity in one message, but real misinformation and disinformation often involve more than confusion. They can include fabricated images, synthetic audio, coordinated campaigns, advertising systems, and repeated reposting across many platforms. Also, in real cases, a message may be partly true rather than simply misread.

visual.title: Same false claim, different intent
visual.learningObjective: Show that misinformation and disinformation can look similar on the surface, but differ in whether the sharer aims to mislead.
visual.description: A two-column comparison shows one false claim travelling through parallel paths. The left path is an honest mistake; the right path is deliberate deception. Read from top to bottom, then compare the outcomes and response needed in each column.

steps.label: 1. False or misleading content appears
steps.explanation: Both paths begin with a claim, image, audio clip or video that is wrong, manipulated or lacking important context.
steps.visualInstruction: Top row spanning both columns: one source card labelled “False or misleading content” with small icons for text, image, audio and video.

steps.label: 2. Why it is shared
steps.explanation: In misinformation, a person shares it because they think it is true. In disinformation, a person or group shares it to mislead others.
steps.visualInstruction: Second row split into two columns. Left card: “Believed to be true”. Right card: “Shared to mislead”. Use different colours and simple arrow connectors.

steps.label: 3. Spread
steps.explanation: People repost, quote, translate or clip the content. Recommendation systems and group chats can increase its reach whether the original sharing was careless or deliberate.
steps.visualInstruction: Third row in both columns: branching arrows from one card to several smaller audience cards. Add a small note under both: “Spreads quickly”.

steps.label: 4. Effects and response
steps.explanation: Both can cause confusion or harm. A useful response is to verify before sharing, add context, correct clearly, and investigate intent when that matters.
steps.visualInstruction: Bottom row spanning both columns: one outcomes card labelled “Confusion, false beliefs, harm”. Beneath it, a response card with four bullet icons: verify, contextualise, correct, investigate intent.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each column highlights its defining feature: left highlights “no intent to mislead”; right highlights “intent to mislead”.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram compares two paths for the same false claim. First, false or misleading content appears. Then the paths split. In the left column, the content is shared because the person believes it is true. That is misinformation. In the right column, the content is shared to mislead others. That is disinformation. Both paths then spread through reposts and recommendations. Both can lead to confusion, false beliefs and harm. The recommended response in both cases is to verify, add context and correct, while also examining intent when relevant.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-column chart replaces any highlighting. The left column reads: false content, believed true, spread, harm. The right column reads: false content, shared to mislead, spread, harm. A final note below both columns says: verify, contextualise, correct, and investigate intent.

workedExample.scenario: A short audio clip claims that a city vaccination clinic in Nairobi will close permanently on Friday.
workedExample.input: Audio message: “The central clinic closes for good this Friday, so do not bother going next week.”
process: A resident forwards the clip to family because it sounds urgent and uses a familiar local accent.
Another person checks the clinic noticeboard and official social media account and finds the clinic is only closed for one day for maintenance.
Investigators notice the same clip is being reposted by several accounts with captions telling people to distrust official announcements.
The family group shares the correction and deletes the original message from the chat.
workedExample.result: The first forward in the family chat was misinformation because it was shared as a mistaken warning. The repeated reposting by accounts using the clip to undermine trust may qualify as disinformation if the intent to mislead is supported by evidence.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN communications team reviews public posts about a household assessment after seeing claims that the survey proves aid is being cut in one district.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The team needs to separate honest misunderstanding from deliberate deception before drafting a response. That affects whether the priority is clearer explanation, faster correction, platform reporting, or escalation to security and information integrity colleagues.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not paste confidential survey responses, personal data, location-sensitive details, or protection-sensitive information into an unapproved public AI service for analysis or summarisation. Use approved tools, minimise data, and keep human review.

whyItMatters: People often need to act before all facts are clear. False or misleading content can affect health choices, voting behaviour, reputations, safety decisions and trust in institutions. The distinction between misinformation and disinformation helps you choose a proportionate response. An honest mistake may call for clarification and better context. A deliberate campaign may require monitoring, evidence gathering, platform escalation, and stronger risk communication. Generative AI matters here because it can make convincing text, voices and images quickly and cheaply, which can increase volume and make checking slower. But AI is only part of the problem; old-fashioned rumours and edited media still spread widely.

commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. Disinformation involves an aim to mislead. Many false posts are misinformation because the person sharing them thinks they are helping, warning others or repeating something they believe. The content may look the same, so intent has to be assessed carefully.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If AI made the image or voice, it must be disinformation.
commonMisconceptions.correction: AI-generated content can be used for art, accessibility, training or harmless parody. It becomes misinformation or disinformation only when false or misleading content is presented in a way that causes people to be misled. The method of creation is not the whole definition.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: You can always tell the difference by looking at the content.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Usually you cannot. The same image, clip or sentence can be shared by one person who is mistaken and by another who is trying to deceive. To judge disinformation, you often need context such as patterns of behaviour, prior correction, coordination, or evidence of intent.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Misinformation is wrong content shared by people who think it is true. Disinformation is wrong content shared to fool people on purpose.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In information integrity work, misinformation and disinformation are related but distinct categories of false or misleading content. The usual distinction is intent: misinformation lacks intent to mislead, while disinformation includes it. The content may be fabricated, manipulated, wrongly attributed, or presented without crucial context. Distribution can occur through interpersonal sharing, broadcast media, search ranking and recommender systems. Generative AI can lower the cost of producing persuasive synthetic media, but these categories are defined by the content’s falsity or misleading framing and, for disinformation, the actor’s purpose, not by any specific model or platform. The boundary can be difficult in practice because intent is inferred from evidence, not read directly from the content itself.

keyTakeaway: The same false claim can be an honest mistake or a deliberate deception, and that difference shapes the safest response.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best distinguishes misinformation from disinformation?
options: Misinformation is always created by AI, while disinformation is always created by people.
Misinformation is false or misleading content shared without intent to mislead; disinformation is shared with intent to mislead.
Misinformation only refers to text, while disinformation refers to images and video.
Misinformation is harmless, while disinformation always causes serious harm.
quickCheck.explanation: The main distinction is intent, not format, technology or level of harm. Text, images, audio and video can all be involved. Both can be harmful, and both deserve checking and correction.

contested: Definitions are widely used but not perfectly uniform across organisations. The usual distinction is intent, yet some institutions classify related terms such as malinformation differently or apply the labels with different thresholds of evidence.
